title: Règle de prédiction de lésion de la colonne cervicale PECARN (PECARN Cervical Spine)
abbreviations: Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Prediction Rule for Cervical Spine Imaging

how_to_use.why:
- Aide à minimiser l’exposition inutile et potentiellement dangereuse aux rayonnements liés à l’imagerie.
- Contrairement aux autres règles de prédiction des lésions du rachis cervical, cet outil a été spécifiquement développé pour une utilisation dans la population pédiatrique.
how_to_use.when:
- Utilisation chez les patients pédiatriques (<18 ans) se présentant au service des urgences après un traumatisme contondant.
- Cet outil peut guider la détermination de la nécessité et du choix de l’imagerie.
how_to_use.pearls:
- Demonstrated high sensitivity and negative predictive value for clinically significant injuries in the derivation study, making it a useful tool for ruling out cervical spine injuries.
- The original study specifically excluded children with solely penetrating trauma.
- “Substantial” head or torso injuries were defined as those requiring inpatient admission or surgical intervention.
- Additional validation studies are currently in progress to further assess this tool’s effectiveness.
- Although highly sensitive (94.3%), this rule should not supersede clinical concern for cervical spine injury.

next_steps.advice:
- Always consider using the tool in conjunction with other clinical factors; it is meant to assist, not replace, clinical decision-making.
- The original study notes that MRI may be required to clarify cases with a high pretest probability for cervical spine injury, although providing direct guidance was beyond the scope of that study.
next_steps.critical_actions: Children have a higher rate of “SCIWORA” (spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality) than adults; if spinal cord injury is suspected, expert consultation with a pediatric trauma surgeon and/or pediatric neurosurgeon or spinal surgeon is recommended.
next_steps.management:
- Cervical spine protection (cervical collar or other immobilization) should be maintained in children presenting with significant traumatic injuries until evaluated by a qualified physician.
- Do not withhold adequate analgesia in injured children to “preserve” a future neurologic examination.

evidence:
[Leonard et al. (2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38843852/)evaluated children presenting with blunt trauma at 18 centers in the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) who underwent cervical imaging; those with exclusively penetrating trauma were excluded. A total of 11,857 cases were included in the derivation cohort and 10,573 in the validation cohort. The primary outcome of interest was cervical spinal injury within 28 days of the initial injury requiring inpatient admission or surgical intervention. Children with suspected child abuse, those transferred from another institution, or those in whom imaging results were known prior to data collection were also excluded.

The presence of one risk factor in the decision rule was associated with cervical spine injury in 12.7% of cases (RR 8.9). Sensitivity was 94.3%, specificity was 60.4%, and negative predictive value was very high at 99.9%.

This study has several limitations. It may underrepresent older children, as many pediatric trauma centers do not accept field patients older than approximately 14 years, and it excludes certain mechanisms (specifically suspected child abuse). This rule has not been validated in these populations and should be applied with caution. Additionally, conditions that may predispose children to cervical spinal injury (e.g., trisomy 21) are not incorporated into the PECARN rule. Although such children were not excluded from the derivation and validation cohorts, the authors acknowledge that predisposing condition data may be incomplete and that the rule was designed to require only history and physical examination findings.

There is yet to be an external validation study, and it should be noted that both the derivation and validation cohorts were derived from the same dataset. This may limit generalizability. However, the broad coverage of PECARN sites across North America and the large sample size may mitigate potential bias.

The potential advantage of this rule is reduced ionizing radiation exposure, either by eliminating the need for any imaging (clinical “clearance” of the cervical spine only) or by supporting use of lower-radiation modalities (plain X-rays instead of CT). Unlike NEXUS and the Canadian C-spine rules, this rule was derived exclusively in a pediatric population, which strengthens its validity in this age group.

input_schema.label:
# Échelle AVPU

Échelle de conscience simplifiée, utilisée notamment en urgence, en traumatologie et en soins préhospitaliers pour une évaluation rapide du niveau de conscience.

| Lettre | Terme d'origine | Libellé français |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Alert | Éveillé / Alerte |
| **V** | Verbal | Réagit à la voix (réponse verbale) |
| **P** | Pain | Réagit à la douleur (réponse à la stimulation douloureuse) |
| **U** | Unresponsive | Ne réagit pas / Aucune réponse |

**Utilisation :** l'évaluation se fait de A vers U ; le patient est classé selon le premier niveau auquel il répond.
